curriculumDefinition.learningOutcome: Select the smallest reliable motion for nearby punctuation, repeated text, matching delimiters, sentences, and paragraphs
curriculumDefinition.representativeExercises: Delete until a quote; repeat a comma find; change the next search match; delete up to the next match; jump between brackets; move by paragraphs in prose or comments
curriculumDefinition.priorityAndPortability: Core. Search and pair matching remain text-based rather than IDE-semantic, and sentence motions are marked optional

lessons.title: Aim at a nearby character
lessons.objective: Choose between landing on a character and stopping just before it in either direction.

activities.title: Find a character or stop before it
activities.body: Press `f` or `F` to move onto a chosen character. Press `t` or `T` to stop one character before it, which is useful when an edit must leave that character in place.
activities.grammar: f{char} / F{char} → land · t{char} / T{char} → stop short
activities.contrast: `w` follows word rules; find and till aim at literal characters on the current line.

lessons.title: Let a pattern end the range
lessons.objective: Complete an operator with a forward or backward search so a named pattern, not a count, marks where the range stops.

activities.title: End a range with a pattern
activities.body: An operator needs a range, and a search can supply one: `d` followed by `/pattern` and Enter deletes from the cursor to that match. `y` and `c` take the same range, and `?` runs it backward from the cursor. This is where search stops being only a way to move.
activities.grammar: operator + /pattern Enter → range ends at the match · operator + ?pattern Enter → range starts at the match
activities.contrast: A plain search range is exclusive: it stops where the match begins, so the matched text itself survives. Backward, the same rule falls the other way — the character under the cursor is the one left out.

activities.title: Cut each row back to its command
activities.instruction: Remove the environment prefix on each row by naming the command that follows it.

feedback.why: Each search supplied a range that ended just before its match.

provenance.languageRationale: Shell rows carry a repeated environment prefix that a command word ends naturally.

activities.title: Predict where the range stops
activities.prompt: The cursor is on the first character of the line. Which text does a delete whose range ends at the next `compute` match remove?
activities.explanation: A plain search range is exclusive: it ends where the match begins, so the matched text stays in the buffer. That is the boundary to expect whenever a plain pattern finishes an operator.

activities.title: The same pattern will address lines
activities.body: A pattern that ends a range here is the same pattern that addresses lines on the command line in Unit 12, where `:/obsolete/delete` removes the line a search finds, and that selects every matching line in Unit 15. Naming text instead of counting it is the one idea behind all three.
activities.contrast: Real Vim can also move where a search lands: an offset such as `/pattern/e` finishes on the match's last character, which makes the range include the match. That form is real and gets its own practice later; every range in this lesson uses the plain pattern.

activities.contrast: Unlike `n` and `N`, the directions of `gn` and `gN` do not depend on whether the last search began with `/` or `?`.

lessons.title: Move through sentence structure
lessons.objective: Navigate and operate on sentence boundaries in prose, Markdown, and commit messages.
lessons.trackNote: Optional — depends on configuration or file type: sentence boundaries are read from `.`, `!`, and `?`, so `(` and `)` earn their keep in prose, Markdown, and commit messages rather than in code.

activities.title: Move by sentences
activities.body: Use `)` to move to the start of the next sentence and `(` to move back to the start of the current or previous one. A sentence ends at `.`, `!`, or `?` followed by whitespace or a line end.
activities.grammar: ( / ) → sentence starts · d) → delete to the next sentence
activities.contrast: These are punctuation rules, not language rules: an abbreviation ends a sentence as far as Vim is concerned, and code rarely contains sentence punctuation at all.

lessons.title: Choose the smallest reliable target
lessons.objective: Combine nearby character motions, searches, match ranges, and delimiter pairs deliberately.

activities.title: Choose the structural motion
activities.prompt: The cursor is on an opening parenthesis in a nested call. Which command most reliably reaches its matching close?
activities.explanation: `%` follows the matching pair, while `f)` can stop at an inner closing parenthesis.

activities.title: Target the text you can describe
activities.body: Nearby characters, repeated patterns, matching pairs, and prose boundaries each have a motion designed for their shape.
takeaways: `f/F/t/T` target literal characters on the current line; `;` and `,` reuse that target.
`/`, `?`, `n`, `N`, and cursor-word searches retrieve text across the buffer.
`gn/gN` turn matches into ranges, `%` follows pairs, and sentence or paragraph motions follow text landmarks.
`d/pattern`, `y/pattern`, and `c?pattern` hand a search to an operator; the range stops where the match begins.

reference.purpose: Find a literal character on the current line, landing on it or stopping short.
notes: Lowercase searches forward; uppercase searches backward.
Till motions preserve the target character.

reference.purpose: Repeat the last character find in the same or opposite direction.
Search for an explicit pattern and revisit its matches.
notes: n follows the original search direction.

reference.purpose: Search for the word under the cursor without typing it.
notes: g* and g# also match inside larger words.

reference.command: d/pattern Enter · y/pattern Enter · c/pattern Enter · c?pattern Enter
reference.purpose: Complete an operator with a search so a pattern marks where the range stops.
notes: A plain search range is exclusive: it ends where the match begins and leaves the match in the buffer.
Backward with ?, the range runs from the match to the cursor and leaves the character under the cursor in place.
Vim's search offsets, such as /pattern/e, move where a search lands; this unit practises the plain pattern.

reference.purpose: Select or operate on the next or previous search match.
notes: gn is always forward and gN always backward.
They can complete operators such as cgn and cgN.

reference.purpose: Jump to the matching parenthesis, bracket, or brace.
notes: On earlier text, percent first finds the next delimiter on the line.
The behavior is text-based rather than IDE-semantic.

reference.purpose: Move to previous or next sentence starts.
notes: A sentence ends at `.`, `!`, or `?` followed by whitespace or a line end.
As an operator range, `)` reaches the next sentence start, so `d)` takes the trailing space with it.

reference.purpose: Move backward or forward across paragraph boundaries.
notes: Empty lines form the dependable paragraph boundaries used in this unit.
